title: AI and jobs
subtitle: A threat, or the next wave?
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Every technological revolution has frightened people about work. But generative AI is the first to reach **knowledge jobs**, not just physical strength.

hero.hook: Machines have already replaced arms. Are they about to replace brains?

blocks.text: Will artificial intelligence destroy millions of jobs, or create new ones? The question has come back with every big technological leap for two centuries.

What is new this time lies elsewhere: AI no longer replaces only physical strength, but tasks we thought belonged to the human mind, like writing a text or reviewing a case file. This course traces that old fear and looks at what has really changed.

sections.title: A fear as old as the machine

blocks.text: The fear that machines will replace people is not new. In the early 19th century, [[The Luddites (1811-1816)]], British textile workers, smashed the mechanical looms that threatened their craft.

blocks.caption: In the 19th century, the Luddites attacked the machines that threatened their trade

blocks.text: Every big technological wave has followed the same logic: it destroys some jobs and creates others elsewhere. The shift from farming to industry cut farmers from 40% to 2% of the workforce in a century, without causing permanent unemployment, because those workers moved into new sectors.
The word “sabotage” is said to come from French workers who threw their wooden shoes, called sabots, into the gears of machines to jam them, though the exact origin of the word is still debated.

sections.title: A break: AI comes for knowledge work

blocks.text: [[Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI)]] marks a real change, because it no longer just follows rules set in advance: it creates original content. Classic computing replaced repetitive tasks like data entry. Modern AI can write, analyze a contract, compose music, even help make a medical diagnosis.

blocks.caption: Generative AI is taking on tasks we thought only the human mind could do

blocks.text: That versatility exposes [[white-collar workers]] above all, people in service jobs whose main working tool is analysis. Recent reports put lawyers, writers and financial analysts among the roles most exposed to the change.
In 1950, Alan Turing predicted that a machine might one day fool a human by imitating thought. Some AI systems have since been credited as co-authors on real scientific patents.

sections.title: A copilot rather than a replacement?

blocks.text: A more optimistic view sees AI as an assistant rather than a replacement. By automating the dullest tasks, like background research or summaries, it would leave professionals more time for the human, ethical and strategic side of their work.

New jobs are already appearing, such as the [[Prompt engineer]], who knows how to word precise instructions to get the best out of an AI. A doctor helped by AI does not disappear: they can follow more patients with more precision.

The worrying part is the speed of the change. Earlier industrial revolutions spread over decades, which left time to adapt. The AI shift is happening in a few years, and that can open a skills gap many workers will struggle to close.
How this change ends will depend above all on the political choices that come with it. Lifelong training becomes essential to help workers move toward new skills.

The debate about sharing the wealth machines create is also back. If AI produces more with fewer workers, how do we fund our welfare systems? That is why the idea of [[Universal Basic Income (UBI)]] is gaining ground, not as a utopia but as a serious safety net.
Some also propose a tax on the use of artificial intelligence, to offset the fall in payroll contributions. In the end, AI pushes us to rethink the place of work itself in our lives.

Earlier industrial revolutions destroyed jobs while creating others elsewhere. Generative AI is the first to threaten cognitive and creative tasks at the same time, which makes adapting more urgent than ever.
